title: The buffering role of perceived servant leadership in the association between attachment avoidance and contextual job performance
content:
by Martin Seitl, Daniel Dostál, Roman Mraček

Attachment avoidance, characterized by deactivation strategies that prioritize self-reliance over collaborative engagement, has been identified as a negative predictor of contextual job performance. However, the situational conditions that mitigate this relationship remain understudied. Drawing on trait activation theory and adult attachment theory, this study examines the buffering role of perceived servant leadership, an attachment-responsive behavioral repertoire conceptualized as a potential situational distractor, in the association between trait-like workplace attachment avoidance and contextual job performance. Using a cross-sectional employee self-report design, we examined a sample of employees in the Czech Republic with measures of workplace attachment avoidance, perceived servant leadership, and two facets of self-reported contextual performance: job dedication and interpersonal facilitation. Hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling with latent variables and a product-indicator approach to interaction. Results showed that attachment avoidance was negatively associated with both performance facets, whereas perceived servant leadership showed positive main effects. The Avoidance × Servant Leadership interaction was statistically significant for both job dedication and interpersonal facilitation, revealing a consistent buffering pattern: the negative association between attachment avoidance and self-reported contextual performance was weaker at higher levels of perceived servant leadership. These findings support the proposed buffering role of perceived servant leadership at the level of conditional associations. However, the cross-sectional design does not establish that servant leadership caused the observed attenuation or that the theoretically proposed mechanisms account for it. The study therefore provides initial evidence to support future longitudinal, dyadic, and experimental research testing whether servant leadership can function as an attachment-focused organizational intervention and examining the processes through which it may shape the attachment avoidance–performance association.
author: Martin Seitl
